analysis.one_liner: Repeals the Affordable Care Act and its companion health-and-student-loan law in full, restoring prior law.
analysis.headline: Senator Cruz introduced the full repeal with 41 Republican cosponsors, but it never got a committee hearing or a floor vote and died when the 113th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have erased the Affordable Care Act and the Health Care and Education Reconciliation Act of 2010 as if they had never passed. That means the insurance market rules protecting people with preexisting conditions, the Medicaid expansion, the tax credits that help people buy coverage, the Medicare drug and tax savings, and the taxes on high earners and health industries would all be rolled back. It would also undo the law that ended federally subsidized private student lending.
analysis.who_benefits: Wealthiest households, who would stop paying the Medicare surtaxes on wages and investment income added by the 2010 laws; medical device makers, who would stop paying the 2.3% excise tax; and private banks and lenders, who would regain the federally subsidized student loan business the 2010 law ended. Some health insurers would also regain freedom from the ACA's rules and fees, though they would also lose the subsidized customers the law brought them.
analysis.who_benefits_short: High earners, device makers, private student lenders

how_it_helps.text: The bill repeals the ACA and the Health Care and Education Reconciliation Act of 2010 in full and restores the laws as they existed before enactment [S2][S3].
Repealing the 2010 laws would remove the taxes those laws imposed, including the taxes on high earners and the health industries that helped fund the coverage expansion [S2][S3].

Repealing the Health Care and Education Reconciliation Act would restore the pre-2010 student loan system, in which private lenders originated federally guaranteed student loans with federal subsidies [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Ordinary people: the roughly 17 million Americans who gained coverage through the ACA's Medicaid expansion and marketplace subsidies would lose it, along with protections for preexisting conditions, free preventive care, coverage for young adults on a parent's plan, and the ban on lifetime coverage limits. People with preexisting conditions would again face denials and higher prices in the individual insurance market.
analysis.who_pays_short: People with preexisting conditions and subsidized coverage

drawbacks.text: The bill repeals the coverage expansion and the insurance market rules of the ACA, so protections including guaranteed coverage for preexisting conditions, dependent coverage to age 26, preventive care benefits, and the ban on annual and lifetime limits would end [S2][S3].

Because the ACA's spending and taxes are tied together, repealing it restores the prior system in which millions of Americans who now receive subsidized coverage through Medicaid or the marketplaces would be uninsured or pay full price [S2][S3].
Restoring the Health Care and Education Reconciliation Act's amendments would return student lending to bank-based federal loan guarantees, which the 2010 law's direct loan program replaced [S2][S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The gains go to a narrow group — high earners, device makers, and student lenders — while the costs fall broadly on people who rely on ACA coverage and protections. An honest supporter would acknowledge the bill offers nothing to replace the coverage and protections it erases.

outcome.mechanism: Senator Cruz introduced the bill and it was read twice and placed on the Senate calendar, but no committee ever took it up, the majority leader never brought it to the floor, and it died when the 113th Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced in the Senate on January 29, 2013, read twice, and placed on the Senate calendar as Calendar No. 9 [S5].
It received no committee assignment, no hearing, and no floor action for the rest of the 113th Congress [S5].
42 Senate Republicans — the sponsor and 41 cosponsors — put their names on it, including the Republican leader Senator McConnell [S3][S4].
The bill never received a vote, and the Congress ended on January 3, 2015 without any action [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The people who benefit from the ACA kept their coverage and protections: those with preexisting conditions, marketplace subsidy recipients, and Medicaid expansion enrollees. High earners and the health and student-lending industries that would have gained from repeal are no better off.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: People who kept ACA coverage and protections

for.name: Sen. Ted Cruz
for.what_they_did: Introduced the full repeal bill and named 34 fellow Republicans as original cosponsors [S3].

for.name: 41 of 45 Senate Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it the entire Republican Senate conference minus a few members [S4].

against.name: Harry Reid
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the Senate floor for a vote; it sat on the calendar until the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: All 42 supporters were Republicans; no Democrat signed on, and the bill never reached a vote that would have tested the split further [S3][S4].

industries.note: Repealing the Health Care and Education Reconciliation Act would restore the pre-2010 system of federally guaranteed student loans originated by private banks, putting lenders back between students and their federal loans [S2][S3].
The bill erases the 2.3% excise tax on device sales that the 2010 laws created, at the cost of eliminating the coverage expansion those taxes helped fund [S2][S3].
The bill repeals the Medicare payroll and investment-income surtaxes on high incomes that helped pay for the ACA, a large tax cut concentrated at the top [S2][S3].
Repeal frees insurers from ACA rules, rate reviews, and fees, but strips away the subsidized marketplace customers and Medicaid expansion that brought them tens of millions of new paying enrollees.
Repeal ends the Medicare drug discounts and rebates the 2010 laws imposed, but also ends the new insured patients the coverage expansion created.
Hospitals gave up payment cuts in exchange for the coverage expansion; repeal would restore the cuts while taking away the newly insured patients who reduced uncompensated care.
